newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court denies Wells Fargo appeal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court denies Wells Fargo appeal.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court Monday said it denied an appeal by Wells Fargo and Co of a ruling that slashed the amount of damages the federal government must pay the bank for breach of contract.

The high court let stand a ruling by a U.S. appeals court that Wells Fargo could collect damages for only the $389,423 it actually lost on a transaction involving a government loan- guarantee program.

The appeals court threw out $10.5 million in damages that had been awarded to Wells Fargo for lost profits the bank said it would have earned if its capital had not been reduced as a result of not getting the promised government guarantee.
The appeals court said the loss of interest on additional loans Wells could have made was "too remote and uncertain" and was not a foreseeable consequence of the government's breach.

Wells Fargo sued in 1988, charging breach of contract after the U.S. Agriculture Department's Farmers Home Administration refused to follow through on a promised loan guarantee for a $20 million ethanol plant in Kansas built by High Plains Corp.
The company failed to repay the bank $389,423 of its construction loan.

The Washington Legal Foundation, a conservative legal group, supported Wells Fargo, saying the government should not be able to avoid liability for certain foreseeable, direct damages when it breaches a contract with a private party.

It said the appeals court ruling was contrary to a Supreme Court decision in July that held the government liable for breaking its contract with thrifts after Congress in 1989 changed the rules for savings and loan institutions.

Wells Fargo urged the Supreme Court to hear the case, citing the "unfair and lopsided result" and warning that the appeals court decision leaves the government "free to breach its contracts with impunity."
But the high court sided with the Justice Department and denied Wells Fargo's appeal without any comment or dissent.
